flow.does: Recall what happens when wood burns
Teach where and when the fire started
Recall key facts from the teaching
Apply learning to two firefighting problems
Apply spread knowledge to new streets

title.heading: The Great Fire of London
title.lead: What can you see when wood burns?

picture.shows: A colour reconstruction of the Great Fire of London, with wooden houses burning beside a London street
picture.subject: generic

slides.heading: The fire begins
slides.lead: The Great Fire started on 2 September 1666. It began in Thomas Farriner’s bakery in Pudding Lane, London.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of the outside of Thomas Farriner’s bakery in Pudding Lane as fire begins inside at night
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Wood feeds the fire
slides.lead: Many London houses had wooden frames. Wood burns, so these frames gave the fire more fuel.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of a London house in 1666 with its wooden frame visibly burning
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Across the street
slides.lead: London’s streets were narrow, with houses close together. Flames could reach from one wooden house to the next.

figure.shows: A reconstruction showing flames reaching between the upper floors of wooden houses across a narrow London street in 1666
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Why did narrow streets help the Great Fire spread?

options.why: Confuses the fuel supplied by wooden house frames with the narrow streets that placed houses close together.
Thinks closely packed houses formed a barrier rather than allowing flames to reach the next house.

slides.heading: Buckets of water
slides.lead: Londoners threw water onto flames using leather buckets. Water cooled the flames and helped put them out.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of Londoners throwing water from leather buckets onto a small burning doorway during the Great Fire
figure.subject: generic

slides.heading: Make a gap
slides.lead: Londoners pulled down houses to make gaps. With no wooden houses in a gap, flames had less fuel.

figure.shows: A reconstruction of Londoners pulling down an unburnt wooden house with ropes and long hooks, leaving a cleared gap between burning and unburnt houses
figure.subject: generic

items.question: Which London street did the fire start in?
What material made many house frames burn?
What did Londoners throw onto flames from their buckets?
A Londoner throws an empty bucket at flames. Why will this not help?
items.answer: The bucket has no water to cool the flames.

items.question: A house is pulled down, but wood fills the gap. Why could fire continue?
items.answer: The wood in the gap can still burn and give the fire fuel.

picture.shows: Two separate imagined scenes: wooden houses on opposite sides of a very wide street, and a single wooden cottage burning
picture.subject: generic

items.question: Two wooden houses face across a wide street. Why might flames not reach across?
items.answer: The houses are farther apart, so flames may not reach the next house.

items.question: A wooden cottage stands alone. Why can it burn without any nearby houses?
items.answer: Its wooden frame can burn and give the fire fuel.

slides.heading: Use both methods
slides.lead: How could Londoners use water buckets and a gap together to protect houses from an approaching fire?

items.question: How did the 1666 fire start and spread?
items.answer: It started in a Pudding Lane bakery and spread between wooden houses close together across narrow streets.

items.question: How did buckets and pulling down houses stop fire?
items.answer: Water from buckets cooled flames, while pulling down houses made gaps with less wood to burn.
